question: Nature films show things no camera could catch by luck. Which of these famous scenes happened as shown, and which were set up?
answer: Each set-up was made because the real thing could not be filmed: Nanook no longer hunted with a harpoon, no camera can enter a wild polar bear's den, and a lens far off hears nothing. The real scenes look staged for the opposite reason: they are so rare the eye has nothing to compare them with.
move: When a shot looks too perfect, ask how the camera got there.
ask: Which viral clip did I believe without asking how the camera got there?

items.note: Paws crunching on snow, heard as a long lens watches from afar.
items.verdict: Mostly added later by sound artists. A lens far away records no sound.

items.note: Killer whales hurl themselves onto a beach to seize sea-lion pups.
items.verdict: Real. Orcas at Punta Norte, Argentina, do it every year, then wriggle back.

items.note: Nanook of the North, 1922: an Inuk hunts with a harpoon.
items.verdict: Staged. He hunted with a rifle by then; the director asked for the old way.

items.note: A fish spits a jet of water to knock insects off leaves.
items.verdict: Real. Archerfish shoot down insects resting above the water.

items.note: Frozen Planet, 2011: cubs born in an Arctic snow den.
items.verdict: Filmed in a den built at a Dutch zoo. A wild den can't take a camera.

items.note: Buffalo save a calf from a pride of lions and a crocodile.
items.verdict: Real. Tourists on safari filmed it in 2004.

reference: Erik Barnouw, Documentary: A History of the Non-Fiction Film, Oxford University Press, 1993; BBC, Frozen Planet, 2011
